```{r setup}
library(here)
library(tidyverse)
library(knitr)
library(kableExtra)

here::i_am("README.qmd")

# kableExtra styling is LaTeX-only; the GitHub README build takes plain pipe tables.
latex_out <- knitr::is_latex_output()

# kableExtra's styling verbs emit LaTeX and have no meaning under gfm, where the same
# table renders as a pipe table. Each call site says what LaTeX alone gets.
latex_only <- function(k, f) if (latex_out) f(k) else k

# value_paper is the string the published page prints and must stay one: read as a
# number, a published "0.80" comes back as 0.8 and the precision it was printed to
# is gone.
gt <- read_csv(here::here("ground_truth", "aronow_etal_2015_ground_truth.csv"),
               col_types = cols(value_paper = col_character(),
                                claim_type = col_character(),
                                defect_locus = col_character(),
                                evidence = col_character(),
                                notes = col_character(),
                                .default = col_guess()))

published_claims <- read_csv(here::here("ground_truth", "published_claims.csv"),
                             col_types = cols(.default = col_character()))

published_tables <- gt |> filter(str_detect(table_figure, "^table_(\\d+|a\\d+)$"))
prose_claims <- gt |> filter(!str_detect(table_figure, "^(table|figure)_"))

manifest <- read_csv(here::here("original_manifest.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE)

# Written by run_all.R, so anything this report says about how long the run takes is
# the measurement from the run that produced the numbers beside it.
timings <- read_csv(here::here("run_timings.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE)
step_seconds <- function(name) timings$seconds[timings$step == name]

fa1 <- read_csv(here::here("maintained", "output", "figure_a1_placebo_i_power.csv"),
                show_col_types = FALSE)

# The Figure A1 grid as the script that built it recorded it, so the report's
# description of the simulation cannot drift from the simulation.
grid_spec <- read_csv(here::here("maintained", "output", "text_figure_a1_grid_spec.csv"),
                      show_col_types = FALSE)
sims_per_cell <- grid_spec$value[grid_spec$claim == "Simulations per grid cell"]

scripts <- list.files(here::here("maintained"), pattern = "\\.R$")
n_scripts <- function(prefix) sum(str_starts(scripts, prefix))

# The English words this report uses for small counts, so that a count and the word
# for it cannot come apart.
in_words <- function(n) {
  words <- c("one", "two", "three", "four", "five", "six", "seven", "eight", "nine",
             "ten", "eleven", "twelve", "thirteen", "fourteen", "fifteen", "sixteen",
             "seventeen", "eighteen", "nineteen", "twenty", "twenty-one", "twenty-two",
             "twenty-three", "twenty-four", "twenty-five")
  if (n >= 1 && n <= length(words)) words[n] else format(n, big.mark = ",")
}
```

*Drafted by Claude Opus 5 under the supervision of Alex Coppock.*

This repository holds the actively maintained replication code for Aronow, Coppock, Crawford and Green (2015), together with the reproducibility report that documents what the original archive did and did not do. It is part of a program applying the maintenance proposal in Peer, Orr and Coppock (2021, *PS: Political Science & Politics*, doi [10.1017/S1049096521000366](https://doi.org/10.1017/S1049096521000366)) to a set of published archives.

| | |
|---|---|
| Article | [10.1093/jssam/smu023](https://doi.org/10.1093/jssam/smu023) |
| Replication archive | [10.7910/DVN/29984](https://doi.org/10.7910/DVN/29984) |

**The data are not redistributed here.** The deposit is `r round(sum(manifest$bytes) / 1024)` KB across `r in_words(nrow(manifest))` files and lives at Harvard Dataverse, which is the only copy this repository points at. `download_original.R` fetches it and verifies every file on checksum and on byte size, and stops if `original/` holds anything the manifest does not list; `original_manifest.csv` pins the file identifiers, sizes and checksums, so the exact bytes this code was written against are recorded in version control even though the bytes themselves are not.

**Repository layout.** `maintained/` is the maintained rewrite: one script per published table or figure, writing to `output/`, which is committed so a reader can compare a fresh run against it without downloading anything. `ground_truth/` ties every published number to the code that produces it. `published_claims.csv` is the transcription: every numeric token in the article and the online supplement, read off the page and classified by hand. `run_archive.R` runs the deposited scripts in a scratch copy and records what they compute, and `build_ground_truth.R` joins the transcription to that run and to the rewrite's own output. `maintained/in_text_claims.R` then prints every claim the article makes in prose beside the sentence that makes it, recomputing each number from the same output files by a path independent of the ground truth's. `original/` is created by the download script and is deliberately absent from the repository. This file is the reproducibility report, also available as a PDF in `report/`.

**License.** CC0 1.0 Universal, matching the terms of the deposit this repository maintains. See `LICENSE`.

**To reproduce.** Clone or download the repository, open `aronow_etal_2015.Rproj`, and run:

``` r
source("run_all.R")
```

That fetches the deposit, verifies its `r in_words(nrow(manifest))` files, produces every table and figure into `maintained/output/`, runs the deposited scripts in a scratch copy, rebuilds the ground truth, prints every claim the article makes in prose beside the number the pipeline computes for it, and verifies the deposit a second time so that a script that damaged it during the run is caught by the run itself. Required packages: tidyverse, patchwork, here, knitr and kableExtra for the rewrite and the report, plus xtable, lmtest and lattice, which the deposited scripts load and which the verification steps therefore need. All are on CRAN, and lattice ships with R. Paths resolve through `here`, so nothing depends on the working directory. A successful run overwrites `maintained/output/`, which is committed: **`git diff` on that folder is the reproduction check.**

The run is dominated by one step. The tables and the two prevalence figures take a few seconds each; the Figure A1 power simulation covers `r format(nrow(fa1), big.mark = ",")` grid cells at `r format(sims_per_cell, big.mark = ",")` simulated experiments apiece and took `r round(step_seconds("figure_a1_placebo_i_power.R") / 60, 1)` minutes of the `r round(sum(timings$seconds) / 60, 1)` the whole run took on the machine described at the end of this report. `run_all.R` writes its own timings to `run_timings.csv`, so those two figures are measurements from the run behind this page rather than remembered ones.

# Summary

```{r summary_setup, include=FALSE}
n_claims <- nrow(gt)
n_archive_match <- sum(gt$match == 1, na.rm = TRUE)
n_archive_fail <- sum(gt$match == 0, na.rm = TRUE)
n_rewrite_match <- sum(gt$match_rewrite == 1, na.rm = TRUE)
n_rewrite_fail <- sum(gt$match_rewrite == 0, na.rm = TRUE)
n_tables <- n_distinct(published_tables$table_figure)
n_table_claims <- nrow(published_tables)
n_text_claims <- nrow(prose_claims)
n_descriptive <- sum(gt$claim_type == "descriptive")
n_pipeline <- sum(gt$claim_type == "pipeline")
a2 <- read_csv(here::here("maintained", "output", "text_figure_a2_archive_grid.csv"),
               show_col_types = FALSE)
a2_cells <- a2$value[a2$claim == "Cells where both grids are defined"]
a2_gap <- a2$value[a2$claim == "Maximum absolute difference from the deposited grid"]
a2_strict <- a2$value[a2$claim == "Maximum power the N = 100 panel gains from strict = TRUE"]
a2_both_na <- a2$value[a2$claim == "Cells undefined in both grids"]
sampler <- read_csv(here::here("maintained", "output", "text_placebo_i_sampler.csv"),
                    show_col_types = FALSE)

# The Monte Carlo standard error of one Figure A1 cell.
mc_se <- function(p) sqrt(p * (1 - p) / sims_per_cell)

power_claims <- gt |> filter(str_detect(claim, "^Power at (200|800) admitters"))
# The main text and the appendix read one of these cells twice, so the distinct
# cells are what the report describes.
power_cells <- distinct(power_claims, claim, value_rewrite)

sizes <- read_csv(here::here("maintained", "output", "text_sample_sizes.csv"),
                  show_col_types = FALSE)
t3 <- read_csv(here::here("maintained", "output", "table_3_study_a_prevalence.csv"),
               show_col_types = FALSE)
```

Two questions, answered before the detail.

## Does the deposited archive run?

Not as deposited. Three things stand in the way, and the third is a bug in the deposited code rather than a stale path or a forgotten package.

All four analysis scripts open with a `setwd()` to a directory that exists on nobody's machine. Two of them name the first author's home folder in 2015; the other two call `setwd()` with no argument at all, which parses and then fails. Every script stops on its first line. Commenting the call out and running from the archive root is enough for two of the four, and those two then run clean. `ACCG_list_replication_experiment.R` needs one more thing: it calls `xtable()` seven times and never loads the package, which the script beside it does load.

The fourth, `ACCG_list_placebo_I_power.R`, needs three further edits, and one of them is a defect in the deposited source file rather than in the caller. `list_simulator()` in `ACCG_list_source.R` reads its p-value with `placeboI_test(...)$p_value`, but `placeboI_test()` returns a named numeric vector, and `$` on an atomic vector is an error in every version of R there has ever been. The function therefore fails on its first call, which means the deposited code cannot have produced the published Figure A1. The power script also calls `listsimulator()`, which does not exist under that name, and passes dot-separated argument names to a function whose formals are underscore separated. With all three fixed, the script runs to completion.

None of this changes a published number. `r n_archive_match` of the `r n_claims` recorded claims reproduce from the deposited scripts and `r if (n_archive_fail == 0) "none fails" else paste(n_archive_fail, "fail")`; the remaining `r sum(is.na(gt$match))` cover quantities the deposited scripts never compute, which is most of them, since the deposit prints tables and states nothing in prose.

## Does the maintained rewrite reproduce the paper?

Every number in a published table does, as does every number the article states in prose, except the readings it takes off one figure. `r n_rewrite_match` of the `r n_claims` recorded claims match the page at the precision the page prints, `r n_rewrite_fail` do not, and `r sum(is.na(gt$match_rewrite))` state no number to be compared against, being either the `r n_descriptive` claims the article makes about shape, sign or count, or quantities it describes without printing. All `r n_table_claims` cells of the `r n_tables` published tables match, as do the sample sizes, ranges and effect magnitudes stated in prose.

The `r n_rewrite_fail` that do not are all readings of one figure, and the fault lies with what the deposit can establish rather than with either the rewrite or the article. Section 4.1 and Appendix C take power off the Figure A1 grid at `r in_words(nrow(power_cells))` points, one of which both passages state, and give the answers as "about 30 percent", "approximately 80 percent" and "80% power". The rewrite's simulation puts those points at `r str_flatten_comma(sprintf("%.1f", sort(power_cells$value_rewrite)), last = " and ")` percent, so all but one of them prints something else at the precision the page uses. A grid cell is `r format(sims_per_cell, big.mark = ",")` simulated experiments, so its standard error at power 0.8 is `r round(100 * mc_se(0.8), 1)` percentage points, wider than the last digit either passage prints, and the deposit sets no seed, so the published figure is one unlabelled draw. `r sum(gt$on_rounding_boundary, na.rm = TRUE)` of these points falls exactly half a printed digit from the page and rounds either way. The claims are right to the precision they can be made at and cannot be checked to the precision they are written at.

The four figures print no numbers, so each is checked against something other than the page. Figures 1 and 2 are drawn from the Table 3 and Table 6 output files rather than recomputed, so the check is that the plotted values are those values, and the build stops if they are not. Figure A2 is analytical, so the deposited script is run and its grid compared with the rewrite's cell by cell: the two agree to `r signif(a2_gap, 2)` across all `r format(a2_cells, big.mark = ",")` cells where the power calculation is defined, and the `r in_words(a2_both_na)` cells where it is not are the same ones in both. Figure A1 is a Monte Carlo simulation for which the deposit sets no seed, so it can be reproduced only up to simulation error of about `r round(mc_se(0.5), 3)` at power 0.5; the rewrite seeds each of its `r format(nrow(fa1), big.mark = ",")` grid cells separately, which makes it reproducible run to run and independent of the number of cores available.

# Paper overview

**Citation**: Aronow, P. M., Coppock, A., Crawford, F. W. and Green, D. P. (2015). "Combining list experiment and direct question estimates of sensitive behavior prevalence." *Journal of Survey Statistics and Methodology*, 3(1), 43-66. DOI: 10.1093/jssam/smu023

**Summary**: List experiments protect respondents from having to admit a sensitive behavior directly, at a heavy cost in precision, because the estimate is a difference in means between long and short lists. The paper's point is that the direct question and the list experiment can be combined: under Monotonicity, subjects who answer "Yes" to the direct question are known to hold the attitude, so the list experiment only has to estimate prevalence among the subjects who answered "No". The combined estimator takes the direct question answer at face value where it is informative and uses the list experiment on the remainder, and its sampling variance is substantially smaller than the conventional list estimator's.

Two Mechanical Turk experiments test it, each crossing question order with five parallel list experiments and direct questions. Study A asks the direct questions first, Study B asks the lists first, and subjects are assigned at random between them, so the design is factorial and the order effect is itself estimable. Three of the five items are not sensitive (nuclear power, public transportation, CNN) and two are (whether Spanish speakers should be discouraged, whether Muslims should not teach in public schools). The main experiment has `r format(sizes$n_complete[sizes$experiment == "main"], big.mark = ",")` complete cases and a replication ten months later has `r format(sizes$n_complete[sizes$experiment == "replication"], big.mark = ",")`. Reductions in estimated sampling variance run from `r round(min(t3$var_reduc))` to `r round(max(t3$var_reduc))` percent. The paper also proposes two placebo tests: the first checks that the list experiment estimate equals one among self-identified admitters, and the second checks that the list treatment does not change the direct question answer, which it does for nuclear power and for CNN in Study B.

# Original archive reproducibility

```{r repro_table}
tibble(
  Script = c(
    "ACCG_list_source.R",
    "ACCG_list_main_experiment.R",
    "ACCG_list_replication_experiment.R",
    "ACCG_list_placebo_I_power.R",
    "ACCG_list_placebo_II_power.R"
  ),
  Status = c(
    "Sourced by three of the four scripts; list_simulator() errors on every call",
    "Stops on setwd(); clean afterwards",
    "Stops on setwd(); then calls xtable() without loading it",
    "Stops on setwd(); then three further errors",
    "Stops on setwd(); clean afterwards"
  ),
  Resolution = c(
    "placeboI_test(...)$p_value becomes [[\"p_value\"]]",
    "Comment out setwd(); run from the archive root",
    "Add library(xtable); the library(lmtest) call is unused",
    "listsimulator() becomes list_simulator(); N.trueadmitter and the other dot-separated arguments become underscore separated",
    "Comment out setwd()"
  )
) |>
  kable(
    booktabs = TRUE,
    col.names = c("Script", "Status on current R", "Resolution"),
    caption = str_glue("Original archive reproducibility, checked against R {getRversion()} on {format(Sys.Date(), '%e %B %Y') |> str_trim()}.")
  ) |>
  latex_only(\(k) k |>
    kable_styling(latex_options = c("hold_position", "scale_down"), font_size = 7) |>
    column_spec(1, width = "3.5cm") |>
    column_spec(2, width = "4cm") |>
    column_spec(3, width = "4.5cm"))
```

Every package the archive names is still available: `xtable` and `lmtest` from CRAN, `lattice` with R itself, and `parallel` in base R. None is unmaintained and none needed substituting for availability. The rewrite drops `xtable` and `lattice` on grounds of output format rather than survival, and drops `lmtest` because the script that loads it never calls it.

## The three errors in the power script

The interesting failure is not the paths. It is that `ACCG_list_source.R` deposits a function that cannot execute:

``` r
reject_null <- as.numeric(placeboI_test(V=V, Z=Z, Y=Y)$p_value<0.05)
```

`placeboI_test()` returns `c(est = , se = , p_value = , n = )`, an atomic vector with names, and `$` is not defined on atomic vectors. Every call to `list_simulator()` raises "$ operator is invalid for atomic vectors". The published Figure A1 exists, so the code that made it was not the code that was deposited; somewhere between the analysis and the deposit the function was rewritten to return a vector and its one caller was not updated with it.

`ACCG_list_placebo_I_power.R` then compounds the problem twice over. It calls `listsimulator()`, which nothing defines, and it passes `N.trueadmitter`, `N.falseconfessor`, `N.withholder`, `N.innocent`, `pr.listliar` and `pr.designaffected` to a function whose arguments carry underscores. Either error alone would stop the script on its first grid cell.

All three are unambiguous naming and indexing slips rather than analytical choices, so the maintenance run fixes them and the rewrite reimplements the simulation from the same specification. Once fixed, the deposited script runs to completion and produces a Figure A1 that looks like the published one. It is not run as part of this repository's pipeline, because it sets no seed and so returns a different grid every time it is called: there is nothing in one draw of it for the rewrite to be compared against. What the rewrite is compared against instead is set out under *The sampler changed underneath the simulation* below.

## No seed anywhere

The deposit sets no seed in any script. Two of the four scripts are deterministic and it does not matter. The third, `ACCG_list_main_experiment.R`, computes five chi-squared tests by Monte Carlo with `simulate.p.value = TRUE`, but none of those five p-values appears in the published Table 2, so nothing is at stake. The fourth is a Monte Carlo power analysis over `r format(nrow(fa1), big.mark = ",")` grid cells at `r format(sims_per_cell, big.mark = ",")` simulations each, and there the absence of a seed means the published figure cannot be reproduced cell for cell by anyone, including the authors. At power 0.5 the standard error of a cell is `r round(mc_se(0.5), 3)`, which is invisible at the resolution the figure is drawn, so nothing the appendix argues from the figure turns on it. It does put the appendix's one numeric reading of the figure, 80 percent power at 800 admitters, beyond what a single grid can settle. The rewrite seeds every cell.

## The sampler changed underneath the simulation

R 3.6.0 replaced the algorithm behind `sample()`, and the Figure A1 simulation calls `sample()` four times per simulated experiment, so a 2015 analysis cannot be re-run under the current default and get the draws it got then. `text_placebo_i_sampler.R` runs a coarse slice of the first panel under each sampler from identical per-cell seeds and measures the gap. Across `r nrow(sampler)` cells the mean absolute difference is `r round(mean(abs(sampler$difference)), 4)` and the largest is `r round(max(abs(sampler$difference)), 3)`, against a simulation error of `r round(mc_se(0.5), 3)` for a single cell and `r round(mc_se(0.5) * sqrt(2), 3)` for the difference of two. The sampler change is therefore not distinguishable from ordinary simulation noise here, and since the deposit sets no seed, neither sampler reproduces the published figure cell for cell in any case. The rewrite keeps the current sampler, which is the correct one.

## What the archive writes where

`ACCG_list_main_experiment.R` and both power scripts write their PDF output into the working directory with bare relative names: `StudyA.pdf`, `powertiles.pdf`, and so on. None of those names collides with a deposited file, so running the archive in place would not overwrite the deposit. It is still never run in place. `run_archive.R` and `text_figure_a2_archive_grid.R` each copy what they need into a scratch directory, and `run_all.R` verifies `original/` against the manifest both before the run and again after it, on every published checksum and on byte size, refusing to proceed if the folder holds a single file the manifest does not list.

# Checksums

All `r in_words(nrow(manifest))` deposited files verify. MD5 is the only algorithm Harvard Dataverse publishes for this deposit, and the manifest records it twice: `md5_published` is what the repository displays, `md5_served` is the MD5 of the bytes `?format=original` actually returns. The two need not agree, and elsewhere they do not; here they agree with each other and with the local copy for every file, and every file matches its recorded byte size. No file in this deposit was ingested as tabular data, so there is no derived `.tab` representation and no UNF, and the ambiguity behind disagreeing checksums cannot arise.

No hash of a file this repository produces is quoted anywhere in this report. A PDF records the time it was written, so the figure PDFs in `maintained/output/` hash differently on every run and any checksum quoted for them would be unreproducible by construction.

# Number-by-number comparison

```{r gt_summary}
gt |>
  summarize(
    claims = n(),
    archive = sum(match == 1, na.rm = TRUE),
    rewrite = sum(match_rewrite == 1, na.rm = TRUE),
    .by = table_figure
  ) |>
  mutate(order = as.integer(str_extract(table_figure, "\\d+")),
         appendix = str_detect(table_figure, "_a")) |>
  arrange(appendix, order) |>
  select(table_figure, claims, archive, rewrite) |>
  kable(
    booktabs = TRUE,
    col.names = c("Table", "Claims", "Archive matches", "Rewrite matches"),
    caption = "Published claims by table, against the deposited scripts and against the maintained rewrite."
  ) |>
  latex_only(\(k) k |> kable_styling(latex_options = "hold_position", font_size = 9))
```

Every published number in the article and its online appendix is recorded: the `r sum(gt$table_figure == "table_1")` crossing counts of Table 1, the `r sum(gt$table_figure == "table_2")` covariate balance cells of Table 2, the `r nrow(published_tables) - sum(gt$table_figure %in% c("table_1", "table_2"))` estimates, standard errors, p-values and sample sizes of the `r in_words(n_tables - 2)` analysis tables, and the `r n_text_claims` claims the two documents make in prose. The published value was read off the article and appendix PDFs and never taken from a script run, which is what makes the comparison worth anything.

The extraction that produced it is exhaustive rather than selective. Every numeric token in both documents was pulled with its surrounding context and classified by hand. Four kinds occur: `r sum(published_claims$claim_type == "pipeline")` the pipeline must reproduce, `r sum(published_claims$claim_type == "descriptive")` claims about shape, sign or count that have no number of their own, `r sum(published_claims$claim_type == "structural")` facts about how the study or the simulation was built, and `r sum(published_claims$claim_type == "definitional")` design parameters such as the payment rate and the assignment probability. Nothing in this article is transcribed from another paper, which is the fifth kind. Searching for numbers by pattern rather than extracting all of them is how a claim in prose goes uncovered, and the prose is where the largest gaps in this pass were.

Figures 1 and 2 carry no printed numbers: they are bar charts of the Table 3 and Table 6 estimates with 95 percent confidence intervals. The rewrite draws them from `table_3_study_a_prevalence.csv` and `table_6_study_b_prevalence.csv` rather than recomputing, so the figure and the table cannot come apart. Figures A1 and A2 print no numbers either. Rows for all four appear in the ground truth carrying a blank published value and an NA verdict, which is what an unprintable claim honestly looks like; the checks that can be made on them are made as assertions inside `build_ground_truth.R`, so a figure that stopped agreeing with its source stops the build.

One caption in the online supplement is wrong, and it is a labelling error rather than a numerical one. Table A4 is headed "Study A (Direct First): Placebo Test I" and prints Placebo Test II: its estimates are centred on zero rather than on one, and its sample size is the full Study A sample in every row rather than the count of admitters, which is what the Placebo Test I table above it reports. Every cell of it reproduces. The rewrite writes it as Placebo Test II, which is what it is.

## What the article says in prose

`maintained/in_text_claims.R` prints every claim the two documents make in prose, in the order a reader meets them, with the published sentence quoted verbatim beside the number the pipeline computes for it. It reads the same output files `build_ground_truth.R` reads and does its own filtering, unit conversion and rounding, so the two arrive at each claimed number by separate routes and a disagreement between them is itself a finding. `build_ground_truth.R` gates the pairing in both directions: a published claim with no block in that file stops the build, and so does a block naming a claim the article does not make.

The `r n_descriptive` descriptive claims are the ones a table of numbers cannot hold. "Each cell in the table contains approximately one-quarter of the subjects", "reductions tend to be larger when a larger number of subjects respond Yes", "none of these differences are significant", "one of five fail in Study A, whereas three of five fail in Study B": each asserts something about a distribution rather than stating a value, so each is checked by printing the distribution rather than by computing a verdict. Three of them needed quantities no published table reports. The article's joint test of Placebo Test I "via Fisher's method" is reported without a value, the comparison of the original experiments against the replication appears in no table, and the counts of placebo test rejections are stated four times across the Results, the Discussion and Appendix F without ever being tabulated. `text_placebo_summaries.R` and `text_original_vs_replication.R` build all three from the published tables' own output.

The float list this coverage is measured against is enumerated from the article and the online supplement rather than from what the pipeline produces, and `build_ground_truth.R` stops if a published float has no row. One float is exempted, and it is the only one. The article prints its own Appendix A.1 with a Table A1 giving the wording of every list question and every direct question, and there is nothing in it to reproduce. Note that the number is reused: the Table A1 the online supplement prints, and the one the rewrite and this report mean throughout, is the factorial comparison of Study A against Study B.

# Maintained rewrite

The rewrite lives in `maintained/`: `r in_words(length(scripts))` scripts, being `helpers.R`, `r in_words(n_scripts("clean_"))` cleaning step, `r in_words(n_scripts("table_"))` published tables, `r in_words(n_scripts("figure_"))` figures, `r in_words(n_scripts("text_"))` that carry the quantities stated in prose and the two checks the wordless power figures need, and `in_text_claims.R`, which prints each of those quantities beside the published sentence that states it. It is a translation, not a reanalysis. Every estimator, specification and sample restriction is the one the paper used.

The deposit's own `readme.txt` claims Tables 1 to 8, Table A1 and Figures 1 and 2 from one script, Tables A2 to A8 from a second, and Figures A1 and A2 from the two power scripts. The rewrite covers all of it: `r in_words(n_scripts("table_"))` table scripts and `r in_words(n_scripts("figure_"))` figure scripts, one per published float, and nothing the deposit claims is missing.

## Architecture

`helpers.R` carries the packages and the paper's estimators. Those estimators are closed-form expressions derived in sections 3 and 4 of the article rather than regression calls, so they are carried over verbatim: replacing them with `lm_robust` would change what is being computed rather than how it is computed. What `helpers.R` adds is one function per published table shape (`prevalence_table()`, `placebo_i_table()`, `placebo_ii_table()`, `factorial_table()`), each mapping the estimator across the five list experiments, so that each table script is a read, a filter and a write, and the five-item loop is written once instead of `r in_words(n_scripts("table_"))` times.

`clean_listdirect.R` reads both deposited CSVs and applies the complete case restriction the article describes. Each table script reads one of the two resulting frames, filters to Study A or Study B, and writes one CSV. The two prevalence figures read the tables they illustrate. The two power figures depend on nothing but `helpers.R`.

Table 1 is rebuilt as a matrix crossproduct of condition indicators rather than as twenty-one calls to `table()` glued together with `cbind` and `rbind` and then reordered by hand twice. Table 2 is rebuilt with `pivot_longer` and `count` rather than five parallel `prop.table` blocks. Both reproduce the published tables cell for cell.

## Deprecated patterns replaced

```{r replacements_table}
tibble(
  Original = c(
    "`rm(list = ls())`",
    "`setwd(\"/Users/Alex/...\")`",
    "`read.csv()` / `subset()`",
    "`with()` over positional columns",
    "`xtable()` printed to the console",
    "`pdf()` / `dev.off()` to the working directory",
    "`barplot()` + `arrows()` + `legend()`",
    "`lattice::levelplot()`",
    "`makeCluster()` + `clusterExport()` + `parSapply()`",
    "`ifelse()`",
    "hand-built `rbind` / `cbind` matrices",
    "`library(lmtest)`, never called"
  ),
  Replacement = c(
    "(omitted)",
    "`here::here()`",
    "`read_csv()` / `filter()` / `drop_na()`",
    "named columns through `str_glue()` lookups",
    "`write_csv()` to `output/`",
    "`ggsave()` to `output/`, PDF and PNG",
    "`ggplot2` with `geom_col` and `geom_errorbar`",
    "`ggplot2` with `geom_tile`, assembled by `patchwork`",
    "`mclapply()` over grid cells, one seed per cell",
    "`if_else()`",
    "`crossprod()`, `pivot_longer()`, `count()`",
    "(omitted)"
  )
) |>
  kable(
    booktabs = TRUE,
    col.names = c("Original pattern", "Replacement"),
    caption = "Deprecated patterns and their replacements in the maintained rewrite."
  ) |>
  latex_only(\(k) k |>
    kable_styling(latex_options = c("hold_position", "scale_down"), font_size = 8) |>
    column_spec(1, width = "6cm") |>
    column_spec(2, width = "6.5cm"))
```

## Two choices worth stating

The archive's `power.prop.test` call passes `strict = TRUE` in three of Figure A2's four panels and omits it in the N = 100 panel. `strict` counts rejections in the wrong tail, and dropping it lowers power by up to `r round(a2_strict, 3)` along the diagonal where the two rates are close. The inconsistency is almost certainly an oversight, but the published figure was drawn with it, so the rewrite carries it forward rather than tidying it away. Reproducing the paper and improving on it are different jobs.

The Figure A1 simulation is parallelised over grid cells rather than over simulations. Parallelising the other way round, forking a process for each of the `r format(sims_per_cell, big.mark = ",")` simulations inside a cell, spends nearly all of its time creating processes; one core per cell with the `r format(sims_per_cell, big.mark = ",")` simulations inside it ran the whole four-panel grid in `r round(step_seconds("figure_a1_placebo_i_power.R") / 60, 1)` minutes for this report. Drawing each cell's seed from a single seeded stream up front makes the result independent of how the work is distributed, which a per-worker seed would not.

# Maintained rewrite verification

The published value in the table below is carried as the string the page prints, not as a number, and a row matches when the archive's or the rewrite's own number, printed to that string's precision, gives the same digits. The comparison is therefore of strings rather than of a number against a tolerance. The distinction matters: as a number, a published `0.80` is indistinguishable from `0.8`, so a tolerance read off the wrong precision would pass anything between 0.75 and 0.85, while a value sitting exactly on a rounding boundary can fail a tolerance it should pass. The string the comparison actually made is written into the ground truth file beside the verdict.

```{r rewrite_verify}
blank_na <- function(x) if_else(is.na(x), "", format(round(x, 3), trim = TRUE))

gt |>
  filter(claim_type != "descriptive") |>
  mutate(
    value_script = blank_na(value_script),
    value_rewrite = blank_na(value_rewrite),
    value_paper = replace_na(value_paper, ""),
    defect_locus = replace_na(defect_locus, "")
  ) |>
  select(table_figure, claim, value_paper, value_script, match,
         value_rewrite, match_rewrite, defect_locus) |>
  kable(
    booktabs = TRUE,
    longtable = TRUE,
    col.names = c("Location", "Claim", "Paper", "Archive", "M", "Rewrite", "M", "Locus"),
    caption = "Ground truth: every published value against the deposited scripts and against the maintained rewrite. Archive and rewrite values are shown to three decimals; the match columns compare at the precision the paper prints, and the locus column says where the fault lies on any row that does not match."
  ) |>
  latex_only(\(k) k |>
    kable_styling(latex_options = c("repeat_header"), font_size = 5) |>
    column_spec(2, width = "5cm"))
```

## Claims the article makes about shape rather than value

The `r n_descriptive` claims below assert something about a distribution, a sign or a count rather than stating a number, so none can be matched against a printed value. Each is checked by computing the distribution it describes and printing it, which is what lets a reader judge the claim rather than being handed a verdict on it.

```{r descriptive_claims}
gt |>
  filter(claim_type == "descriptive") |>
  select(table_figure, claim, evidence) |>
  kable(
    booktabs = TRUE,
    longtable = TRUE,
    col.names = c("Location", "Claim", "What the pipeline finds"),
    caption = "Descriptive claims and the evidence computed for each."
  ) |>
  latex_only(\(k) k |>
    kable_styling(latex_options = c("repeat_header"), font_size = 6) |>
    column_spec(2, width = "4cm") |>
    column_spec(3, width = "8cm"))
```
